utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that we're already in public session. You may continue, Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And what happened on that day, the 24th of May? How did the attack start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, the shelling of Kozarac began.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And what area of Kozarac were you in at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted) because I was off duty that day

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And can you describe what the attack was like, what that was like when the shelling started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Strictly speaking, in Rajkovici you couldn't see anything really, except you could hear it. You could hear explosions, shells exploding. Because Rajkovici is part of the surrounding hillside, so you couldn't really see the attack on Kozarac itself or some targets that were hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you go out to an area to try and observe some of the shelling yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was at a place where you could see from the Kotlovaca area and the hill called Denovica [phoen], where our fields are, and I was in that area and I was able to see a settlement towards Kozarac, and that is what we called Dera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be provided what's been marked as Exhibit 3/88A, B, and C, three photos of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, could you look at those three photos, please, and indicate whether or not you recognise them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise them. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And the other two photos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My house before the war and my house after the war, when it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could the first photo be put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we should switch the ELMO on, Mr. Usher. We're not getting any picture over. Yes, we have it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I recognise that the glare appears to be pretty bad on that. I don't know if we can adjust the mirror angle or something. I think it will be generally sufficient, because everyone has copies of the actual photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, could you point to the area on the hill where you said that you were and from which you could observe the shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And from that location, you indicated that you could see to the hamlet in the area of Dera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's the road towards Kozarac, and the houses along that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you were on the hill looking towards Dera, could you tell what type of structures were being targeted by the shelling, what was being hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were privately owned houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you know the people who lived in those houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And what was the ethnic group of those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During the time that you were observing the shells hitting that village, did you observe any fire coming from the village, or return fire from the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did the people who lived in your area do during the shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came to two shelters. One of those shelters was underneath the veranda of my own house and the other one was opposite the road at my uncle's place in the cellar there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And when you referred to shelters, are you referring to cellars under the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, cellars underneath the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At that time were there any armed soldiers or was there any fighting or return fire coming from your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened the following day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day we were already informed that as a group, and in a column, under a white flag or a white sheet, we needed to go towards Kozarac and abandon their homes, which they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And how were you informed? How did you receive those instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were people who were listening to the news on a transistor radio, or a small radio which worked on batteries. And then they passed on this news that there would be no shelling, that there would be no problems, that people should move peacefully and in an orderly fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were these instructions broadcast over the civilian radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did your family follow those instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't have a transistor radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I meant once you were advised by your neighbours, did you follow the instructions? Did you get in a column and move down towards Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: About how many people were in your group, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 50 and 100. I don't know exactly. I didn't really pay attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: As your group was moving down towards Kozarac, what did you see along the way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we were leaving my village, there was a pool of blood on the road where they said that a man had been killed. Then as we entered Kozarac itself, near the city mosque, there were also two or three pools of blood, not really pools but blots, and they said that a column of inhabitants from Brdjani had been shelled there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And what about the homes and buildings along the way? What state were they in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were destroyed. Some were still burning. The smoke was coming out, with just the outside charred walls standing. It was a terrible sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you know the people who lived in those homes that you saw along the way that were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And what ethnic group were those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers, any Serbian forces, along the way as you went from the area where you lived down towards Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be provided with Exhibit 376, please. That's the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan, I think it is Exhibit 3/76. I see on the transcript "Exhibit 376."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm told I may have given the wrong number. I'm looking for the map of the Prijedor area.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Is it 3/77?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could be. No. It's a map about this big of the Prijedor area. 1/26. I have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I was right about that. Sorry. Exhibit 1/26. It was marked incorrectly. I apologise, Your Honour. We need the top half of the map, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, could you please locate on the map the area in which your village is? No, no. You can remain seated. Just point, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened when the column that you were in reached Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is where we had the first encounter with the military. That is where they were waiting for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And when you say you had an encounter with the military, they were waiting for you, can you describe that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those soldiers were stationed in a building where the TO of the Kozarac local community used to be housed. A flag was hoisted, the three-colour flag. Nothing else. We had no problems at all. They just let us pass further down towards the elementary school, where we waited as the other columns from the surroundings of Kozarac arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened then while you were waiting at the elementary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the elementary school, in front of it, on the road. We waited to see where people would be going, because they hadn't told us that we would be going in the direction of Trnopolje. After a few hours of waiting, we headed towards the crossroads of Trnopolje. At that spot, the men were separated from the women and children, and their column went towards Sucici, whereas the women and children stayed behind waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military police were there, and they separated me and two other members of the TO of the Kozarac local community. They put us in a military vehicle, the so-called Pynzgauer and took us to Koncari. They asked about our personal data. Then from there we went on to the Prijedor barracks, probably for a checkup, to see who we were and what we had been doing. Then after a brief stay in the barracks, we were returned to the military police checkpoint at Kozarusa, where the commander of the military police was a certain Jovic. After our personal data were taken down once again, we heard an announcement of a radio station where somebody was intervening. He said "by civilians." So they didn't question us any longer but took us back in the same military vehicle to Keraterm, but the drivers who were taking us there made certain provocations. They threatened me, saying what they did to women, that they first have a physical abuse, and after that they kill them. I just said, "Don't talk to me like that. You don't know who I am." I reached Keraterm. I entered the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: First, when the soldier in the vehicle said to you -- you referred to it, saying what they do to women, that they have a physical abuse. Could you please describe for the Judges; what term did he actually use?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, but I have to say the same words. "What we do with women like you is," and I apologise again, "we first fuck them and then we kill them so that there should be no witnesses." I don't know the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, during all of this time, from the time that you were picked up in the military police vehicle and you went to these various military stations, what, if any, calls did you hear on the military radios about ongoing fighting or resistance, military resistance, in the Kozarac area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What, if any, signs from the Serbian forces did you see to indicate that there were ongoing battles or resistance? In other words, how were the soldiers acting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was quiet. At the time there was no shelling or anything. They were a bit tipsy, all of them, at the checkpoint. They behaved in a rather -- I don't know how to put it -- an inappropriate manner for a soldier, especially when on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were the soldiers acting as if they were in combat operations; that is, were they moving tactically or were they acting as if they were simply in charge of the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They behaved as if they were in charge, as if -- they didn't have any tactical or military activities. They behaved as if they were at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, what were you wearing on that day when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I show you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This same top in which I was arrested, taken away, and which I wore throughout my period in the camps. And unfortunately, the bottom part, I gave it to a friend of mine who went to Manjaca when the Omarska camp was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could the witness please be provided photographs that have been marked, previously been marked, as Exhibits 3/27 and 3/34. Show those to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, do you recognise those photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, when you say "Keraterm," do you mean by that the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the buildings we were brought to and where we were for the first day in Keraterm, the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you please put first the photo that shows the area of the building that you were first taken to onto the ELMO so that she could point it out for the Judges. Could you please point to the area of the camp where you were first taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the building, and this is the entrance [indicates]. I went in through this doorway and I waited downstairs in the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was that a reception area for the -- what used to be the factory, Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was the Keraterm factory. It was a newly built facility of Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And when you first arrived at the camp, were there any prisoners on the area outside of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And what happened to you once you were inside the reception area of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I entered, somebody came up. I don't know his name. I would be able to recognise him if I saw him. A shortish man, with greyish hair. And he went in front of two other members of the TO. He started with his provocations. He was staring at us, walking around us. "We need little birds like that. You didn't need to do that. Why did you have to do all that?" That kind of thing. Provocative questions and behaviour. It didn't really affect me much. Each time I looked him in the eye, he had to bend his head down, so he just couldn't provoke me. After that I was called in upstairs to one of these offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And what happened --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and there were three interrogators sitting there. One was asking the questions, another one was taking things down, and a third was listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, did you recognise any of these interrogators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know them from before, but later I learnt that among them was Drago Meakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where did you later learn his identity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learnt it in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you see Drago Meakic later in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of -- sorry. Please finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came on a visit, but I would not see him there on a daily basis. I don't remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of uniform were the interrogators wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly they wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And when you say "camouflage uniforms," what colour camouflage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in different shades. They were not the same. Some were in green tones, others were in blue. So they were not all identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did any of the interrogators tell you who they worked for; that is, were they police, were they military, or some other organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they tell you why you had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I still keep wondering why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of questions were you asked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the questions, except that they said I should have been in their ranks -- I don't understand that -- that I should have been on their side. Which side is that, and why was I with the Muslims? It is a nation of the former Yugoslavia, so I can't understand that. And that that nation was against the Serbs, and again I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they tell you what was going to happen to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They should all be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you physically mistreated in any way during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not in Prijedor; in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were they taking notes, preparing notes, during this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They were writing things down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you allowed to read the notes or were you shown the notes after the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you asked to sign a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When the interrogation was concluded, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took me to one of the premises of the warehouse in Keraterm. I think it was number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you please place that photograph on the ELMO and point to the area for the Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is right here, or one of these, anyway. One of these premises [indicates]. There are several entrances, and I was put in one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And were there other prisoners already in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were. It was quite full already. They were all men, mostly from Kozarac, among those I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And of those you knew, what was their ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Muslims, and a couple of Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you the only woman in the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During the time that you were in the Keraterm camp, did you see any of the Serbian forces or authorities who you later saw also in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was Drago Radakovic, and I noticed, passing, somebody I recognised there as well, and that is Drago Prcac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And where did you see Drago Prcac while you were in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He just passed by me up the stairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there any other women in the Keraterm camp during the time that you were held there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was in that room, I didn't know of a single other woman. In the evening, when they told me to go on, that I couldn't stay there with those men, that I should go elsewhere, I came to the same building again; that is to say, I went into the hall again, and there was a woman waiting there. I didn't know her. I didn't know who she was. But she was just waiting there like me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And were you taken out of the Keraterm camp that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They took me to the police station in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And the police station in Prijedor, is that commonly referred to as the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you learn the name of the -- did the other woman who you saw in the hall waiting, did she go to the police station with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And did you learn her name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Velida Makmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And do you know where she was from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened once you arrived at the police station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was again searched to see whether I had anything on me. The person who searched me -- that is to say, I was forced to take my clothes off and remain in my underclothes so that they could check to see whether I had any weapons on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who was the person who conducted the search?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a woman. And her name was Miroslava Grahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you interrogated at the police station in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We were just transferred later on to a separate room where we were supposed to spend the night, and that was the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you placed in a cell alone, the two women, or were there others in the cell as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the condition of the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the word "cell" itself speaks for itself. It stank of urine, it was dark, it was stuffy. There were no proper windows, just like a sort of iron bar, and you couldn't get any light through that aperture at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you given any food or water that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No water, but I think we got a tin of some kind by way of food. I don't think we ate it, but we did not get any water, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you physically mistreated in anyway while you were in the police station or in the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were not mistreated, but we heard different comments coming from outside. And it wasn't an easy thing. We heard them saying that we ought to be raped and what they were going to do to us, but none of that was done. They were just provocations, verbal ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day they took us out, and one of the policemen, the guards, took us up to the restaurant where we had lunch. We were given a portion of beans. We waited there to see where we were going to be taken after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And where were you taken after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, we went downstairs to the yard, the courtyard of the SUP building, where a police car was waiting for us, and I can say that it was a Black Marija sort of thing. And the driver, one of the policemen who was in charge there, he put us and three men inside and took us over Gomjenica, Tomasica, Grudica, across the hill to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened once you arrived in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we reached Omarska, we were searched again in the same way, that is to say, a little differently. We stood up against a wall and had to raise our hands up with three fingers pressing against the wall, and we had to stand astride so that they could feel us up our legs to see if we had any weapons, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who was present from the camp staff when you arrived at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was Zeljko Meakic, and at that particular moment, some people were coming out of the building; that is to say, they were the interrogators. I recognised Dragan Radakovic as being one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, was anything said specifically to you and Velida Mahmuljin when you arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was a surprise for them to see women arriving, but I just heard them say, "What are we going to do with these two whores? Why are they here? We ought to kill them." Something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you know who said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was Zeljko, Zeljko's expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And Zeljko's last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Meakic, Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you later learn what -- what did they do with you after you arrived at Omarska camp, you and Velida?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we waited downstairs again for a time at the entrance to that administrative building, and afterwards, we were taken off again in a Mercedes to the police station in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you recall who accompanied you in the Mercedes to the Omarska police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was the driver, and Zeljko Meakic was with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened once you were at the Omarska police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljko took our particulars down there. We said who we were and everything else, and he wrote that down in the black book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of questions did he ask you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He asked what our names were, our date of birth, where we lived, what nationalist party we belonged to, and why we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you physically maltreated in any way during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was Velida physically maltreated during her interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Omarska, at the police station, no, she wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you ever informed, while you were at the Omarska police station, why you had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where did you spend that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the cell in the prison. Zeljko asked whether we would like to stay in one of those -- in one of their offices or would we like a separate room, but I, for one, didn't know what "a separate room" meant and what it referred to, and Velida didn't either. He said "a separate room." So once again we were transferred to the prison and that cell there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And that cell was in the Omarska police station itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you receive any food or water that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you physically maltreated during the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And what happened the next morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next morning, when they opened the cell door, it was sunny. It was a fine day. We stepped out of the darkness, and I found it hard to see because the glare of the sun was in my eyes. Then one of them, whether he was a soldier, a policeman, or someone like that, he hit me with his rifle butt here [indicates], and Zeljko reacted and said, "Don't beat her," and cursed them, swore at them. He said, "Take them into the car." We went into the same Mercedes and went off to the camp again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What happened on your return to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We waited there at the entrance again, in a room where there was some lockers for clothing. That's where we waited to be interrogated or whatever. I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you taken for interrogation at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was Velida taken for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Velida was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When Velida came back from interrogation, what did you notice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I noticed that she was frightened. She had signs of physical abuse; that is to say, she had a bruise on her forehead which she skilfully hid with a lock of hair. She was red all down here in the lower part of her face. What happened to her, I don't know. When I saw her I said, "What happened to you?" She just looked at me and started crying and didn't say anything, which means she was physically abused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During those first few days that you were in Omarska, where were you held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were in one of the offices, one of the rooms on the first floor of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you spend both day and night in that room on the first floor or were you moved somewhere else during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. At night we were in that room, but in the morning, at 7.00, we had to go downstairs to the restaurant, the catering -- the canteen, and we would have a table and chairs. So when you go inside the restaurant, this was to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could beg your indulgence. I intend to have the witness only refer to all the areas that are relevant to her testimony on the model at one time, because it will have to be in closed session so that she can get up and move around. So she will fully describe these areas but later in the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we'll have an easier solution, and that is to have a longer pointer perhaps. Then the witness could use that longer pointer and point from where she's sitting. That would -- she wouldn't have to get up and lose her protective measures. So we're now going to go into private session so that the witness can approach the model and point to what she has to point to. Let's go into private session then. I beg your pardon, Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was actually going to wait and do it near the end when she's discussed all of the relevant areas and then she can just do it all at once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that's a good idea, but perhaps we could prepare this, because the registrar has lots of things at his disposal. Perhaps we could get a longer pointer with which the witness could point to the model, but I think your suggestion is a good one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We'll check on the break if that can be arranged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're continuing in public session. Thank you, Mr. Keegan. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, you described that you spent the days, when you first arrived at the camp, in the restaurant area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At that time, could you see where other prisoners in the camp were being held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at the beginning, because they were taken off straight away to other rooms where they were shut up and they didn't go out of them, but I could just see them coming to lunch in columns. But where they all were, I was not able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How long were you in the camp before you began to serve food to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps 15 to 20 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And prior to that time, who served food to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The food came ready-prepared from the kitchens probably. They prepared the food. But the meals would arrive already cooked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And for the first 10 to 15 days, who served the meals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three men who had the duty of serving the meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After that first period, once you began serving meals to the prisoners, did you continue to work in the restaurant the entire time that you were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, except when there would be a visit of some kind, towards the end when the journalists arrived, and then the women didn't show themselves and it was the men who served the meals again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You say the women didn't show themselves. By that do you mean you voluntarily stayed in a room someplace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We had to be elsewhere. We were not able to -- they didn't allow us to show ourselves. They didn't want people to know that women were there, because they kept denying that there were any women at all in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you know how the food was delivered to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be brought in -- I don't know -- in some kind of vehicle. It would arrive at about 9.00 and would be distributed until late in the afternoon, 3.00 or 4.00, 5.00 p.m. perhaps, depending.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was food brought for both the guards in the camp and the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the difference between the food for the prisoners and the food for the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I had occasion to try that food too, thanks to, once again I say, some good people among them. There were some good people, and so on several occasions us women received that other food. They offered us some. They asked us whether we were hungry, and they gave us this food, their food. And the food that the prisoners were given, there was a drastic difference between that food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you please describe what was the daily meal for the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning, the daily meal was far better than it was later on, in the latter period, when it was terrible. It was -- there was no salt in it, no spices or anything like that. What can I say? I can tell you that it was all without any salt at all in it, so you can image the taste it had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During the first period, then, what was the type of meal that a prisoner would get each day? What did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning there were beans. There were enough beans. It was a consistent bean stew. And there was rice, and they put some meat in as well. It was a far better quality than it was towards the end. And when I asked, "What's this you're giving us now," well, they said, "We haven't got enough to eat either, and that's what we're giving you."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, this first meal you're describing, you say there were enough beans, it was a consistent bean stew, and then you talk about rice and some meat. Were those separate courses, or are they all in one soup or stew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was separate. Each time they tried to give us a different -- different things to eat, so it was different food. It was on different occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So one day it would be bean -- soup with beans in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And on another day the soup would have rice in it; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Or it would be cabbage or something else like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they also receive bread with this soup each day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning they would get a quarter of a loaf, and afterwards an eighth of a loaf. But for a very short period of time were we given this quarter loaf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you say "a very short period of time," how many days are you talking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. I don't know. The conditions were such that you couldn't really take note of all these details. It wasn't important for us. We just kept thinking why we were there and how we could get out, so we didn't pay attention to details of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, you say that the food then got worse. How was it worse? What was it like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was more rarefied, more liquidy, not as many spices. They didn't put any salt into this to give it taste. It was awful, and you could see the effects of it on us prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was the food for the prisoners, that is, the vegetables that were in the broth and the water, were they always of fresh quality or were they spoiled vegetables on occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the prisoners, well, very often the beans would be sour already because of the hot weather, and they would bring the same food back and distribute it again, and the beans had gone off. And very often you would sense this smell. And they gave this to people, and people would get dysentery and have stomach problems afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were prisoners given adequate time to eat their meals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was a very short period of time that we were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there always enough food for all of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Many of them -- no. Many of them would remain hungry. There wasn't enough for them. Many of them didn't even dare come to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why wouldn't they dare come to eat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because of the beating in coming and leaving that restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were the prisoners given anything to drink with their meals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They received water in the latter part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, you say when they received water in the latter part, you mean they got cups or glasses of water with their meal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was on the table. There were pitchers of water on the table with plastic glasses, or the water had already been poured into the glasses, or they would pour the water from these pitchers themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you say the latter period, what period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the last month or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is this after the journalist visited the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prior to their visit and following their visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, what was the food like that the guards received? You referred to it, but you didn't describe it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, normal food, good quality food, caloric food. It wasn't the same every day, but it was far, far better compared to the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they receive meat in their meals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Vegetables?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Potatoes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Bread?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were they given only soup every day, the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 3/70, A through D. That's the four photographs of the prisoners going to and coming from meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, can you please look at those four photographs. Witness B, what do those four photographs depict? What do they indicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bringing in of the prisoners to lunch. The way they took their lunch, left their plates, and went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Okay. This first photograph which you've placed on the scene, does that indicate how the prisoners would proceed into the canteen, the restaurant, for their lunch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And is that the serving line we see in the back of that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Here you see it [indicates]. That's the serving line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next photograph is when they took their meals off the line and took their spoons, cutlery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And do you recognise anybody in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise Zoran Delic, one of those who distributed the food. That's him there [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And did he supervise the food distribution during the time that you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next photograph is when they would return their empty plates. And the bread that they didn't have time to eat, they held in their hands. And you can see this on the photograph. They would take this bread out with them and eat it later on. Where they all were, I don't know. Some of them were on the pista; others were in the garages, in the "white house," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The guard who's standing on the left of that photograph as we look at it, what type of uniform is he wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the uniform of an active-duty policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And the next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the way out of the restaurant. And behind you can see the "green house" area, the glass area [indicates], which is where some of the prisoners were also positioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Okay. Just for clarification's sake, we've got different translations there of that term. That area in the background, what was it called where the prisoners -- you can see the prisoners sitting down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Green house."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Glassed-in area. Interpreters note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Your Honour, would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Keegan. This is a good moment for the pause. And we're going to have a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Keegan, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, how were the guards in the Omarska camp organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were organised in three shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And how often did the guard shifts change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was able to register what was happening, I noticed that the shifts changed every 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there anyone in charge of each of the guard shifts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who were the shift commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mladjo Radic, Milojica Kos, and Momir Gruban.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you know any of those three from before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I knew Mladjo Radic or, rather, Mladen Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of uniforms did the guards wear in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were various uniforms, camouflage, SMB, olive green, or police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown what's been previously marked as Exhibits 3/69A and B, and what was admitted yesterday as Exhibit D26/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, can you look at all three of those pictures, please. If you could place what is actually the second picture in the stack that you have on the monitor first. Witness B, first of all, do you recognise the person in that picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And who is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mladen Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of uniform is he wearing in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A police uniform, summer uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever observe Mladjo Radic wearing that uniform during the time he was a guard shift commander in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He wore it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you place the next photograph on the ELMO, please. The guards in that photograph, what uniform are they wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first two are wearing police uniforms, whereas this other one, I think he has camouflage trousers on, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of shirt is that third individual wearing, the one you described as wearing what you think are camouflage pants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seems to me to be a white shirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Would you place the third photograph on, please. Witness B, first of all, do you recognise the person in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Drazenko Predojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What position did he hold in the camp, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you know whose shift he was on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Mladen Radic's shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of uniform is Predojevic wearing in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His shirt is olive grey and the trousers are camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing him wear such an outfit in the camp when he was a guard there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever have any direct contact with Drazenko Predojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would, during lunchtime, most frequently be in the restaurant, in the dining-room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Earlier you described beatings which occurred as prisoners came in to eat and when they left. Do you recall ever seeing Drazenko Predojevic take part in those beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Frequently in the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was he also involved in other beatings in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, whenever he was on duty. He was one of those that I noticed in particular and of whom I could say that he was one of the worst.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he ever ask you to give him medical treatment of any type?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I bandaged his hand here [indicates] in the area of the wrist, or I would put a Band-Aid on a finger he may have hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And how did he get those injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he tell you how he got them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He just said, "Come on. You're from the medical corps. Show me what you can do and bandage my arm."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who were the command staff at the Omarska camp in the first period during which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljko Meakic and, well, Miroslav Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you know either of those two men before you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What position in the camp did Miroslav Kvocka have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Judging by his behaviour with the guards and the personnel, the guard personnel, at the very beginning it was quite evident that the guards gathered round him and then they would disperse to take up their positions. And judging by those conversations that he had with the guards, one could conclude that he had a senior position in the camp, one of the senior positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you able to tell from the conduct of the camp personnel that you observed, or conversations which you overheard, whether he was in a position superior to the guard shift commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Several times I heard a guard addressing him in passing as "chief" or "commander." Everyone addressed him as a person who was responsible for the command in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How often did you see Miroslav Kvocka in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't really say, but almost every day during his stay there. At first I saw him quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did Miroslav Kvocka carry a weapon of any type?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was known by his pump-action rifle and his black gloves with the fingers cut off, and that is how I remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you recall what type of uniform, if any, he wore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He wore a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Approximately how long do you recall seeing Kvocka working in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A month, a month and a half. Not more than that. I didn't see him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you able to tell from what you could observe whether Miroslav Kvocka was in a position superior to or below Zeljko Meakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From what you could observe with respect the way the guards treated him, did they treat him in a manner similar to Meakic or differently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After Kvocka left the camp, who worked with Meakic in the command of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Drago Prcac came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What indications did you have that Drago Prcac was a commander in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, by the behaviour of the personnel or the guards, who treated him in the same way they did Miroslav Kvocka. They were -- after talking to him, they would quietly go to their guard posts, and that is how I came to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From what you could observe, did the guards and the camp personnel treat him in the same way they treated Zeljko Meakic or differently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the same way as towards Zeljko Meakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you see Drago Prcac move around the camp area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I would see him every time when he would take up his duties. He would contact the guards. But this was very briefly. Then he would go back or go off somewhere. So he didn't spend a lot of time among the guards. He would withdraw. Whether he went to the offices where they were, or somewhere else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Would he carry anything with him when he walked about the camp and spoke with the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a notebook under his arm. What the purpose of that notebook was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever have an occasion to see Drago Prcac speaking with the shift commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That happened at the pista, within the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see them speaking upstairs on the first floor of the administration building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had occasion to be, not often, but quite frequently, in their office, to make coffee or to clean the offices or something like that. But I wouldn't hear any important conversations, because as soon as I went in, the subject of the conversation would change, so there was nothing of significance that I could overhear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What type of clothing or uniform did you observe Drago Prcac wearing at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would most frequently wear the summer police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And did you see him wear anything else other than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only a civilian shirt or something of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you remember the colour of the civilian shirt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually it was -- well, white.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever have a conversation with Zeljko Meakic about his position in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion -- it was towards the end -- when I heard that they called him chief, or commander, I asked him, "Are you the commander of the camp here?" And he would say, "No. I am commander of the security." And then he would stress that Drago Prcac was the commander of the camp. He told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From the beginning of your stay in the Omarska camp, did you observe prisoners arriving, being brought to the camp, from the restaurant building where you were during the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was precisely where we were sitting, and you could see this from the place we distributed food, because the restaurant had large windows, and you could see that. But the women would sometimes turn their backs, and you couldn't always see. But as I worked every day, almost every day and distributed food, I did have a chance to see what was being done with the prisoners who were brought by buses there or by any other means of transport. Usually it was a police car. But then I had the chance of seeing what was being done to those people, how they physically mistreated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You mentioned when prisoners were brought via police car. Did you also observe occasions when they were brought in larger vehicles such as a van or a bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They would come in larger groups. Then they would come by bus. They would stand usually in front of the garage or behind the kitchen, behind the restaurant, and they would get out there. They would be searched there. That would be the beginning of the beatings, as far as we could hear. Then what one by one, in a column, single file or whatever, they would go into the different premises, into the "white house" or wherever they were distributed. They would move on from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: On those occasions that you observed the arrival of prisoners, who would go out to meet the prisoners as they arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, one of those main ones on duty that day in the camp, then the shift leader and the guards who were present there, who were on duty that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In one of your earlier answers, you mentioned that prisoners would be beaten after they got out of the vehicles and were being searched.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Then you indicated they moved on to various locations in the camp. Would anything happen to the prisoners as they were being taken to those other locations, that you could observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was precisely when they were taken off in the direction of the "white house," where there were -- where it was obvious that they had previously been beaten. They had bruises and visible signs of blows on their faces and so on. When they would go off in the direction of the "white house" one by one, they would be met there by the guards where they would beat them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And would these beatings take place out in front of the "white house" where you could observe them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, precisely so. In front of the "white house." At the entrance of the "white house" itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever overhear the guards talking about what they were doing to the prisoners when they arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember one particular person. When the driver came and the president of the municipality, this Music, when a person ran into the kitchen and said, "We've got a good one here, a big fat one. We'll take out our pleasure out on him." And at the time I said, "Poor Idriz," not knowing that he would come up to me and ask me, "Ah, you know him, do you?" He was from Kozarac and my schoolmate from elementary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In addition to that one specific prisoner that you knew, did you overhear other similar conversations on other occasions where the guards spoke about what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were other comments but there was fear generally. You couldn't hear each and every comment. There would be comments after every arrival, especially the guards, although many of them were quiet. Many of them didn't say anything. Some individuals were even proud when they saw new arrivals, seeing that they could beat them and so on, but it was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, did you ever see any of the camp command staff that you have talked about thus far present when these new arrivals were beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have already said that those who were on duty that day were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you recall occasions when Miroslav Kvocka was present on the pista area when new arrivals were beaten there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I repeat again: All of them, at the time, were outside when the new arrivals came, all of them who were on duty that day, whether it was Kvocka or Prcac, but that staff was outside, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And what about the shift commanders? Did you ever see Radic present when new arrivals were beaten on the pista?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was present as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And Milojica Kos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, depending on whether he was on duty when the group was brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, did you ever see any of those men, whose names have just been mentioned, beat any of the detainees themselves, that is, beat them personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of those men, whose names we have mentioned, try to stop the beatings or to intervene in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, other than these beatings of the new arrivals which you have talked about, were prisoners beaten on all three of the guard shifts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were prisoners in the Omarska camp beaten or tortured every day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the interrogations they were. When it was time for interrogation, then they were beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And at other times were there random beatings of the prisoners in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. I didn't hear it properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At times other than -- you've spoken now of new arrivals and beatings when prisoners were going to meals and beatings during interrogations. On occasions other than those, in other words, you know, just other parts of the day, were prisoners beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when they arrived. That's when they beat them. During their meals they beat them, and during their interrogations they beat them, and during the course of the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you see the effects of these beatings on the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the day you mean? Yes. But at night I just heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, I'm speaking specifically about -- were there any visible signs or marks or injuries that you could see on the prisoners as a result of these beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were signs. For example, on their backs. Their shirts would be torn and you could see that the flesh had been torn. There were bruises on their face, and the arch around the eye might being fractured, or you could see the signs of a beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were all three guard shifts the same in the way that they treated the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In what way were they different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have to say that in Mladen Radic's shift there were most beatings going on. And as far as I was able to notice, there were young men who were quite simply proud of their duty and position in the camp. Why, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you say that they were "proud of their position and duty in the camp," what do you mean? What do you mean "proud"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were -- they put themselves above us. They had this kind of attitude of superiority, arrogant, and pride as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you give an example of what Radic's shift was like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His shift was in one -- a single composition. It was formed of young men; well-built young men; well-developed, strong young men; and as I have already said, they were proud.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you a give an example of an instance when they mistreated prisoners or beat prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, usually it was when they came to lunch, came in to lunch. When the new arrivals came as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you recall one particular occasion when the beatings at lunch were worse than usual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was one particular day when they beat them so much, when the detainees -- when bread would fly out of their hands. They had very little time to come in, get their food, eat it, and go out, and all this would be accompanied by blows. Everyone tried to hold on to his eighth of a loaf of bread. If they were able to put the bread in their pockets, they managed to save the bread, but all the others carrying this bread, when the blows fell, they would open their hands and the bread would fall out of their hands. This was collected up, and then it was said that these people were on a strike, that they didn't want to eat. So that was one of the worst days ever during my entire stay in Omarska, and it really upset me tremendously, and I'll never forget it. Why -- well, they're not cattle; they were human beings -- what the reason was. Well, I heard a day or two later that there had been a conflict at Gradacac and that many people had lost their lives there and that was the reason why they were beating the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, if we can go back and ask a few more questions about that incident. First, let's start with this explanation you gave. You say that there was a battle at Gradacac and that many people lost their lives. Who lost their lives in that battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the people of Omarska, the population of Omarska who were on the battlefront, and that that was the main reason. Now, who they actually were, well, I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: But you were told a couple of days later that the reason for the beating on that day was because soldiers from Omarska had been killed at the front.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was a discussion between some of the guards, and I happened to overhear their conversation in the kitchen while they were talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you remember -- can you recall the date of this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was it about this particular incident, the one you described earlier, that made it so much worse than the beatings that you described that occurred when prisoners were going to meals as a routine? Why was this day so much worse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they had to go in running, and when they entered, they would receive blows at the entrance. And they would go in with these injuries. And one of them, in fact, couldn't even see out of his eye, because blood was trickling down and the arch of his eye had been fractured. And when others heard that prisoners were being beaten, they didn't come in to lunch at all, because they would rather go hungry than receive blows. So that that particular day we had some food left over, and later on that food -- actually, that food was distributed again the following day, the leftover food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You referred to bread flying out of prisoners' hands. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the bread they had, it flew out of their hands, and the guards picked up the bread, the pieces of bread, and took it away. And Zeljko Meakic that evening called me up and -- how shall I put it? I was taken up to their room. He asked me why those people had gone on a hunger strike, why didn't they want to eat? And I just said, "Zeljko, it was not a strike of any kind. They were so angry today, they were in such a rage, that -- they beat them so much that -- and I can't understand that anybody could beat anybody else so much. Why? That day they were in a particular rage."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever have a conversation with Mladjo Radic about that beating, the way the prisoners were beaten that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When he came into the kitchen, I said, "Why are these people being beaten? Why was that done?" And I think he'll remember the sentence. He said, "Oh, fuck them. Who could prevent them from doing it? I can't do anything to stop them."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he refer to the guards in any particular way? Did he call them something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he said something like an unruly crowd, something like that. It's a special word. It didn't have any particular meaning, but like a band or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, when he said this to you, in your opinion did you take it as if he was serious about how he described them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, according to the expression he used, and his face, it wasn't anything serious. I couldn't -- I didn't take him to be serious. He just said it, like -- like a joke, in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From what you saw during your time in the camp, did you believe that Mladjo Radic did have the authority to control the conduct of the guards on his shift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In your opinion, if he had wanted to, could he have prevented beatings that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if he has the duty of being a shift leader, then I also think he has the authority to prevent something from being done as well, or to make a report of it to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Based on what you observed in the camp, if he had given such an order, that is, not to beat the prisoners, do you believe the guards on his shift would have obeyed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope that most of them would, but not all of them. Most of them would have listened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did Mladjo Radic carry a weapon when he was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They all had weapons. He had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, earlier you referred to interrogations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How often were prisoners interrogated in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everyone was interrogated at least once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were interrogations carried out on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you able to hear the interrogations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't hear the actual questions asked by the interrogators, but I did hear the abuse, the blows; quite simply, the cries and screams of the people who went in for interrogation, and the general noise, and shouting at the people who were being interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How often did you hear this abuse, the blows, the cries and the screams of the people who went in? How often would you hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you could hear that often, almost every day during the interrogation sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where would you be when you would hear this noise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If someone was in one of the offices on the first floor, in your opinion would they have heard this noise as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because the insulation of the walls wasn't such that you couldn't hear. It wasn't soundproof.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see the prisoners when they came down from interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall mention one of those examples. I saw, for instance, when they brought down a man who had been beaten, and they held him under his armpits and his feet just dragged along the floor, along the pista. And they would take him off in the direction of the "white house," where he was taken over by two prisoners, and that's where they took him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And what did that prisoner look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't actually see him from the front, what he looked like from face on; I just saw his back and the state he was in when they took him out. He was all beaten up. And they carried him out. He couldn't walk himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever have to go into the interrogation rooms themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We slept in two of those interrogation rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever have an occasion to have to clean those interrogation rooms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only once. I went there with another woman. The two of us were cleaning those two rooms to be able to sleep in them afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: On other days, did other women have to clean the rooms while you were working in the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: On the occasion when you cleaned the rooms, what did the room look like when you went in? What condition was it in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, on the table, on the wooden board, there were blots of blood. On the walls, which was a brick wall, there would drops of blood. There was blood on the floor as well. And behind the door I found a broken pair of glasses with very thick lenses. Who they belonged to, I don't know. And I found some other objects, probably those they used during the interrogations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, what were those objects that you found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a whip made from a plaited strand. Then there were metal bars. What they were used for, I don't know. And on one of those metal bars there were traces of blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Just to clear up the transcript, the translation issue: The whip that you found, was that made from braided wood, strips of wood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was wood which had been cut up into -- I don't know how to explain it -- into several strips and then were braided together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, this metal bar with the traces of blood on it, did you do anything with that metal bar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
