utterances.text: I put all those objects that were on the table into the metal cupboards for clothing. However, one bar fell behind and I didn't pick it up. It stayed there that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And was there an incident the next day that occurred because of that metal bar falling behind the metal cabinet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The question was which women had spent the night there, and they had to be asked why it had been removed. It was Dragan Radakovic who sent for those women, two women. Jadranka Papes and Esma Elezovic went up there, and upon their return, they were afraid. Especially Jadranka was scared. She had known Radakovic from before the war. And then we asked, "Why so much fuss?" And then he said, "If the same thing happened another time, we would be transferred to one of the men's rooms. A message was left for me to pass on to Zeljko, and I gave it to Zeljko and he said to me, "Never mind. He's just talking. Nothing will come of it."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Earlier you referred to prisoners being beaten at night. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard, or rather all the women who were in that room in which I slept could hear when one of the people beaten up in that room was brought in. We heard his cries. We heard the blows. We heard glass shattering and splinters falling to the floor. We could hear the person who was being mistreated. So all the women fell silent. We were all scared. Of course, that night not one of us had a wink of sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there any specific instances where you knew the victim of the beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can mention Simo [sic] Saric and Professor Puskar, Abdulah Puskar, because I heard them and recognised their voices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you repeat the full name of the first man you mentioned, Saric? What was his full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Silvio Saric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, where were you when you heard the beatings of Saric and Puskar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in that room, together with another 17 women who were in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, specifically with respect to Silvio Saric, what could you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can quote the words he spoke when he was being beaten, when he received those blows. They demanded that he admit something and he said, "I'm not guilty, Brothers. Why you are you doing this, Brothers?" And then the answer was, "You Ustasha motherfucker. Who is your brother? If you had been our brother, you would be on our side."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did you hear after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing. For a moment, everything fell quiet. We didn't hear anything or anyone except the words, "Get some water," which meant that the man was unconscious. Then after awhile, they resumed the beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, when you heard Silvio Saric saying the things you just said to the Court, could you tell if they were beating him at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when he said, "Don't do that, Brothers. Why are you beating me? I'm not guilty. I'm innocent."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were the sounds that you heard that indicated that he was being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, simply a blow, blows against these metal cabinets, then the glass shattering and dropping to the floor. All this could be heard, because we women, who were lying down with our ears to the floor, every movement, every step could be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there any curses during that beating that you recognised so that you knew who it was that was saying that to Saric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've already said the curses used. They cursed his Ustasha mother, and they said, "If you were our brother, you would be on our side." I've already said that. At one point in time, I recognised the voice of Zeljko Meakic, but he wasn't alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. We just would like to know what is the right explanation of "Ustasha" in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What does "Ustasha" refer to, Witness B?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, "Ustashas" was the name given to Catholics. For me, it's a derogatory term, similar to the term "Chetnik" when it is used for Orthodox Christians, if that is sufficient as an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it applied only to Catholics or also to Muslims in this context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They called the Muslims Ustashas also or balijas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Just to clarify now the record. When you refer to Catholics, are you referring also to persons who could be described as Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should like to give an explanation for the term I'm using, "Catholic," "Muslims," and "Orthodox Christians." "Catholics" apply to Catholics in Bosnia and a Croat is an inhabitant of Croatia, as the word itself implies. The Croats are also Catholics. When I say "Orthodox," it applies to Serbs or Orthodox people; whereas for me, the word "Serbian" is an inhabitant of Serbia, but in Bosnia, they are Orthodox, because both Serbs in Serbia are Orthodox. Because in Bosnia, there are no Serbs or Croats there. They're Orthodox, Muslim, and Catholic inhabitants. That is my explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan, I should like to remind you. If we are to finish with this witness today, I think that we should have finished by 12.30. As you know, there is the cross-examination, the re-examination, and then the Judges. So please bear that in mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did you know that the victim of that beating was Silvio Saric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised the voice, because I knew him a long time before I came to the camp, many years before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Had you spent a significant amount of time socialising with him over the years before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Most often, we went mountaineering, and we met there at the mountain chalet at Kotlovaca, taking long walks on Mount Kozara. We would organise group outings of members of the mountaineering club where we had gatherings and meetings of mountaineers, and we spent a lot of free time together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Had you seen Silvio Saric in the camp prior to the beating that you've described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when he came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see him after this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you ever told by other prisoners what had happened to Silvio Saric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I reached Karlovac, I was told that he succumbed to the beatings, that he died. How he died, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now with respect to Professor Puskar, how did you know that he was the other person who was being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the same way as before. I heard it. I knew him. He was my math teacher. Mathematics was taught regularly in schools, so I had most contact with him among all my teachers. So I recognised his voice when he raised his voice or spoke quietly as in class. So I remembered his voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see Abdulah Puskar in the camp before this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see him again after this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you told by other prisoners what had happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was also told that he succumbed to those beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you say "succumbed," do you mean he died as a result of the beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you recall a Serb holiday which occurred while you were in the camp, called Petrovdan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. Tyres were set on fire. And I remembered it by an incident that I personally witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did you see then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw a tyre, a large tyre, on fire in front of the "white house," and very thick, black smoke was rising, and some flames from the tyre, and I just saw the legs of a man in that tyre. Who it was, what had happened, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you say you saw the legs of a man in that tyre, was that at the time when the tyre was on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Just when the flame flickered and lit up the area, I noticed the legs. This was just the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you recall whose shift -- which guard shift was on duty at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, did you ever see dead bodies of prisoners in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw, further away near the "white house" and one that was being carried out of the "glass house." It was Dalija Hrnic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting you. The interpreters are asking you to move a little away from the microphone. I apologise. First they ask you to go up to the microphone, now they're asking you to move away. It's a bit complicated to please everyone, as you know. Thank you very much. You can put your headphones in a more comfortable manner. Look what I do. You can adjust them, you see. You can adjust them to make them comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm fine. I was sitting in this way to give my arms a rest, but I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We just want you to feel at ease. You can do what you like with your hands and rest in the best way that suits you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, when you would see the dead bodies in the camp, where would those bodies be, in what area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the area of the "white house." And this one body that was carried out of the "glass house," as I have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That was a person you identified as Dalija Hrnic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During the time that you were in the camp, were the prisoners allowed to bathe? Were the men allowed to shave? Were people allowed to wash their clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At any time were women given the necessary items for their personal hygiene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Only the last month we were given a kilogram of medical cotton wool if any of the women would have their periods. Unfortunately, in my case, after three months of stay in Omarska, I had three periods. There was nothing that I could use except toilet paper for as long as it existed; after that, newspapers. There was nothing. One of their cleaning ladies once, at my request, brought me a few sanitary napkins. Otherwise, as I said, I used paper or newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: These cleaning ladies, as you referred to them, what areas of the camp did they work in? What did they clean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in the administrative building. They were cleaning the offices or whatever. Anyway, they were present there on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they ever clean the areas where the prisoners were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You have described what the food was like at the camp, the hygiene conditions. Did prisoners suffer from disease and illness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was dysentery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You also described the beatings and the effects of those beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown what was previously marked as Exhibit 3/31.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, do the bruises that show in that picture, did they -- are they representative of the types of bruising you saw on the prisoners in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness B, were women called out of their rooms at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall give you my example, when I was taken out. It was at the very beginning. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was during the first ten-day period or so when I arrived. A young man took me out during the night. There was no electricity. There were just us three women then in one of those rooms, myself, Velida, and another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the name of the man --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember now. There were two of them with the same surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we'll come back to that question. Witness B, what happened when this young man took you out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took me to one of these offices, with the intention of rape. He threw me on the floor. I was wearing the same sweatsuit. He lay on top of me and started physically abusing me. I tried to defend myself, and I did for as long as my strength lasted, and at one point, he threatened to kill me if I wouldn't let him have his way. I continued, like any other woman, to fight back. At one point, he crossed his fingers like this and suddenly pulled down, and I felt a very strong pain in the neck area of my spine, and I said to myself if I survived I would report him. And I mentioned Mladjo Radic then. I think it was another -- Brane Boic, a policeman that I also know, or Zeljko Meakic. One of the two. I know that I mentioned one of these two, but I do know that I mentioned Mladen Radic. And he got up, sat at the other end of the table, offered me his hand, and said, "Can we be friends from tonight on?" Which means that people were taken out without the superiors in the camp knowing about it. And he was precisely the guard who was watching over us three women. He was sitting in the corridor. He was responsible, as the guard, for the women.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why did you mention Radic's name? Whose shift was this guard on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first I didn't know. I didn't even know that there were shifts, because this was at the very beginning, when one simply doesn't know anything, out of fear, and is not even interested in what was happening. I mentioned Radic, as he was the only person I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you later learn whose shift this guard was on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That guard, after a certain time, was transferred from there, and I didn't see him at all for a while. He was not there for long as a guard in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were you ever called out at night by Zeljko Meakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would most frequently come during the night to call me to make coffee for them if they were tipsy or somebody was feeling sleepy on duty, and often I would go out. And Zeljko would call me simply to ask me certain things about something, so that I did go out often, both during the daytime, in the evening, and during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: On one occasion did you walk into a room Mladjo Radic was in, by mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, unfortunately. That night I was supposed to go to see Zeljko. I didn't understand where, which room I should go to. And I opened the first door, and when I entered, Radic said, "What are you looking for here?" And I said, "Nothing. I'm looking for Zeljko." However --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Go ahead. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked him why he was there. I think he will remember his answer. He said he was waiting for Jadranka Cigelj. Whether she came or not, I don't know. Anyway, I left, and Zeljko was in the next room. When I told him that Zeljko sat down with me and we talked again, he asked me about various places, where the people of Kozarac may be hiding. That evening I didn't experience anything, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, excuse me. Did Radic say why he was waiting for Jadranka? Did he say anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Whether he was speaking seriously or not, he was rather rude in the words he used, crude. He was cursing her and saying that he would take his revenge. Now, whether he did or not, I don't know, but with me he never was very serious; he was always flippant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, on what day were you released from Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 23rd of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Keegan. We're now going to have a half-hour break before beginning with the cross-examination. But can I know already the order of the cross-examination, or do you wish to discuss it during the break, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the fact that we are having a break, we will have some consultations about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Simic. So we're going to have a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Witness B, you are now going to answer questions put to you by the Defence counsels. Mr. Simic, what is going to be the order of the cross-examination, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that we're beginning with you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and that's why we're sitting up here. The order will be as it is in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do all the Defence counsel have questions to put to the witness? Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, I was just going to inform you and the opposite side that the Defence of the accused, Mr. Kos, will not be cross-examining Witness B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. You may be seated. Mr. Tosic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for you to be able to plan the time for the cross-examination, the Defence of Zigic Zoran will not be asking Witness B any questions either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tosic. Mr. Simic, how long do you expect to take? Mr. Jovan Simic, how long do you expect to take? I see that Mr. Fila is engaged in a conversation. I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some 20 minutes. A maximum of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was talking to Mr. Jovan --

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not sure whether we will be asking any questions at this point. We'll see whether our colleague counsel will raise any of the questions we wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, I apologise for reversing the order. How long?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes. Very well. I see that Mr. Simic is going to say that he needs 20 minutes, more or less; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we'll do our utmost to complete our questioning of this witness today, even if we have to work until 4.00, and I'm saying this without any fear. I know that the interpreters and the other staff are trembling at this point, but I think there are exceptional, extraordinary circumstances where we must all proceed in an extraordinary manner. I don't want to take up too much time in explaining why. So, Mr. Simic, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Madam, I apologise for having to take up some more of your time and take you back to these events, events which are not a happy experience for you, and I hope you'll be able to forget them as quickly as possible without any undue results. During Mr. Keegan's examination, you were shown a photograph and you happened to mention a name, and that name was Zoran Delic. You said that it was a young man who, with two other persons, was in charge of the distributing food while the women detainees were not included in this process. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Delic belong to the guards or some other system, structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he wasn't a guard. He was just present when the food was distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did the other two individuals have this same status until you yourself became part of the system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: As we're talking about the food, let's round off that topic. During your testimony, you said that the only illness in the camp was dysentery, which was the result that the food would be returned that was not used up on the previous day, and as the weather was hot, the food would go bad, and the food would be served up the next day in the camp and distributed to the prisoners. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, was it a common occurrence in Omarska that food -- there would be too much food to be returned to where it is cooked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately -- I have to tell the truth -- it was precisely during those days when the people were beaten, physically abused, the prisoners coming to get the food, and many of them didn't dare come. And I stressed that earlier on. So that was the reason why we had more food left over, food left over, surplus food.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned something with respect to the police, the army, and so on, and you have some knowledge in that respect, and I'd like to ask you something about the relationship between the police and the military. Were these two completely separate systems in their functioning, in the way they functioned? Were they set apart completely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By virtue of the functions in the war? I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you about the organisation of the army and the organisation of the police. Were these two separate organisational systems within one state system, within a community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the police had its functions and activity in the area in which they were, and the army went to the front and it had its functions to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the police and the army were then two separate systems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No. They cooperated.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they cooperated, but in Omarska, for example, in Omarska, the -- it is the Territorial Defence -- not Omarska. I'm sorry. I made a mistake. Not Omarska I mean Kozarac. There was a company of Territorial Defence, I believe you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: And the commander, the leader of that company, could he command -- was he in command over policemen? Could he be their commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I was an ordinary, run-of-the-mill soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: What about the commander of the police? Did he ever command you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we're speaking about Omarska. From your angle of vision, which was from your advantage point at the restaurant, and the buildings vis-à-vis the restaurant, were you able to see roundabout members of the army, members of the Territorial Defence, in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, except for the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You only saw the military guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You brought up the subject of interrogators during your testimony frequently. Now, according to our own terminology, interrogators working on the first floor of the administration building, that's them, do you happen to know who was the superior of these interrogators? To whom did they report to after having had an informative conversation with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Zeljko Meakic on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: And in your statement -- and we'll return back to that statement later on -- you said that before this unfortunate occurrence, he was a professional commander of the police station of Omarska. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go back to the relationship of Meakic towards the interrogators and investigators. The interrogators, did they send any reports to Mr. Meakic with regard to the interrogation sessions, the results of the investigations and so on or did they report elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, you mentioned the situations when new arrivals came by bus, new detainees, and you also said, although you weren't very definite, said that the persons on duty would go and meet them. I'd like to ask you now to tell us where the buses which arrived, where they stopped.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The buses that came with the prisoners usually stopped behind, parked behind the kitchen or in front of the garage of that same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: In view of your status as a protected witness, we're going to try and not have to go out of public session. So from your position sitting down, would you look at the model, take a look at the model in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one here you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The restaurant is the building nearest to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: The garage, as far as I can see, is at the corner, diagonally away from me but closer to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Opposite the garage there is a broad concrete area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That area was called the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: When the buses arrived, where would they stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They stopped behind the restaurant, behind the kitchen, or in front of the garage; that is, looking at it from my side here.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: From your side. I see. You said that in the course of the day, you would be in the restaurant and the area where you sat there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You also said that during the night, you were up on the floor above, in the rooms. Did these rooms look out onto the restaurant or this opposite side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They looked out onto the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: I see. The restaurant. Thank you. Did you, from whichever position, that is to say, the restaurant and the room you slept in, were you able personally and directly to see the buses arriving and people stepping off the buses? Did you see that yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see it myself; I just heard the noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Very well. You heard the noise of buses arriving. Thank you. Would you tell me this then, please, although you've already given an answer, did you ever personally, you personally, with your very own eyes, see Mr. Kvocka being present and attending the arrival of new prisoners at the place where the buses stopped? Yes or no, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Where from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You go down from the room where it says Militia, and he would move in the direction of the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: But a moment ago, we noted that either from your first position or your second advantage point you couldn't see the buses, you could just hear the sound of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I said that he went towards that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You mean by the sound. He went towards the sound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to that question. He went in that direction, but did you ever see him, the bus, the prisoners, and Mr. Kvocka together? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Upon reception of the prisoners who were moving around in the direction of where they would be going, Kvocka would later on be amongst those guards in that circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to Mr. Kvocka later, but let us move on to Mr. Meakic for the moment. You said that he was a professional chief of the police station in Omarska, but during your testimony about the incident that took place (redacted), you said that you gave Mr. Meakic the information, you submitted him with the information, and that your tone was a little harsher in view of what had happened. Could you tell me what Mr. Meakic's reaction was like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at first, when I arrived, or that is to say when he asked me why they were on strike, why they didn't want to eat --

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. You explained all that, madam. You explained it to Mr. Keegan and we understood what you said. But did he undertake anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether he undertook anything, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: No. I asked you did he say anything. That was my question, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I asked him whether there would be any consequences on me if I told the truth, he said, "No. I want to know the truth." What he undertook, what he did after that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: When you were telling Mr. Keegan about your personal experience with the guard whose name you weren't able to remember --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember the name now.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Very well. But Mr. Keegan will probably ask you that question later on, so I'm not going to ask you the name now. You said that you said you were going to report him, amongst others, to Mr. Meakic. Did you, in fact, do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. For purely safety reasons for myself. I was afraid that something would happen to me afterwards if I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Madam, in the course of December, did you make a detailed statement in 1994, a detailed statement concerning the events related to Omarska and also to this particular event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you give that statement of your own free will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Or were you forced to under pressure of any kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no pressure at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you say that that young man was disciplinary -- that there was a disciplinary matter over him and that he was discarded from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Meakic found out, after this dismantling itself, about this incident with this boy, and Velida Mahmuljin told him about that event. I just want you to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, but let me ask you a concrete question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: So at that time when you gave your statement, you did not say that you reported this young man to Mr. Meakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, and I did not report him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: But did you report him at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, afterwards, when Zeljko called me, and that's when Velida reported the incident, not me. Velida reported the incident, and then Zeljko called me to come to him, and he wanted to hear my explanation of what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was just before the disbanding of the camp, when Zeljko called the two of us to ask whether we had had any problems, and I said no; Velida said yes. And Velida then told him, Velida Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether food was prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was prepared down in the workers' kitchen. I think so. But it came ready made, ready cooked.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was in charge of the cooking of the meals, preparation of the meals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: During the time you spent there, and your stay seems to be the longest, unfortunately, did you happen to notice that in Omarska any health workers of any kind came, nurses, doctors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was Dr. Ivic and there was a male nurse. His name was Mico or something, a paramedic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: How often would they come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I saw them just a few times, not often.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know an individual by the name of Ljuban Andzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember him. He only came once, when we women were away from -- discarded from the camp. He came to that place down there where we were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did he bring any medicines, medical aid, hygiene, anything for hygiene, that kind of thing, with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago the women, the cleaning women, cleaning ladies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Were they members of the police or the Omarska company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They just wore civilian clothing. They were just cleaning ladies. They had their own clothes. I don't know what they belonged to, what they were a part of.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: In addition to these women, were there any other civilians who would, on behalf of the Omarska mine company, do any work there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a maintenance man on duty. He was in charge of the installations. There were several mechanics. And they were drivers at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to go back to a portion of your testimony when you said that you saw Mr. Kvocka talking to the guards, the policemen or the reserve police, and that after this discussion they would go off, and that you concluded that he had a certain status in the hierarchy at Omarska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know the system of organisation of the appointment -- nomination and appointment of individuals within the police system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to have any knowledge whatsoever of the fact that in this procedure -- all right, you say you don't know the rules. That doesn't matter. But the procedure, do you happen to know whether Mr. Kvocka had any decision or ruling as to his status? Do you happen to know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand your question. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll be short and precise. Do you know whether Mr. Kvocka had a legal act, a legal document, a ruling, a decision, an order -- we were talking about the army -- by which he had a work post of some kind? It doesn't matter what, but some kind of official work post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: "There," you say. Very well. But do you know whether he had any piece of paper assigning him to any particular duty or post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you personally ever -- I know that there were scenes of this kind, but we're all here to ascertain the truth. Did you personally ever see any beatings, abuse, any -- and did you see Mr. Kvocka standing by and not doing anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When these people, these prisoners, were brought?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the arrivals. You explained that. You said where you were standing, what that looked like, so let's not return to that. But were you ever present, as a witness -- don't be so surprised. You're a witness, so I have to ask you whether you saw. Witnesses see, if you see what I mean. Did you ever see Mr. Kvocka order anybody to abuse anybody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you mentioned that you would often go into the room on the first floor -- it doesn't matter where it is exactly, but it would be opposite your dormitories -- where it said -- up on the door it had the -- it said "militia" on the door, a plaque saying "militia" on the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Now, we both know the set-up of that administration building. Was that the only door that had "militia" written on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: And who were in the other rooms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The investigators, or interrogators. Yes, investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that you would frequently enter that room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You made coffee as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us the dimensions and surface area of the room, roughly? Roughly. I don't want to -- you needn't worry. We don't need an exact figure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about 3 by 3 1/2 metres, or 3 by 4 metres. It was a small room. But there was furniture, there were tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: So 3 by 3, or 3 by 4 metres, which means 10 or 12 square metres, approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please: In that room, what kind of furniture was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two tables with a couple of chairs. There was like a glass cabinet. In the corner there was like a bed, which was used by the people on duty. And there was some sort of a communications equipment, radio or transmitter. I don't know. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: This room, during the day, and we are talking about the period when the investigators were there, the interrogators, did any one of the personnel of the Prijedor police station attend? Did they undertake any kind of activities there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you notice, among these teams coming from Prijedor -- I'm talking about the investigating teams -- were women among them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One was called Nada Balaban.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: And the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lakic, Rada, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so. Her surname was Lakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You don't remember the name Nada Markovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You frequently use the term "on duty," saying that certain persons were on duty in that room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Leaving aside all the other things, was Mr. Kvocka among those who kept duty in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never went to that room when Kvocka was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Meakic have duty service in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a loudspeaker system. Was there any other communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You said a loudspeaker?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: So it was a kind of radio station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Some sort of communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was anyone on duty there with that equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several times I was there when Zeljko Meakic ordered a boy to be on duty there.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that somebody always had to be in attendance there, to be reachable by communications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that Mr. Kvocka left Omarska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know the reason why he left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the information I received is correct, the reason was his two or three brothers-in-law, the brothers of his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: What did you hear about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were staying in his house, apparently, and were later brought to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. He wasn't there anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: I see. He wasn't there anymore. So when his brothers-in-law returned, Mr. Kvocka's brothers-in-law, he was no longer in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: There's just one further point that I -- and I should like to quote from your statement: "In the morning two women asked me in the room why I was dirty and dishevelled. I lied to them. But they knew that I was lying, so I told them what had happened. I did report him, after all, and they withdrew him from his employment."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the time I was taken out during the first ten days of my stay in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I asked you a moment ago whether you reported him to Mr. Meakic, and here you explain that in detail. But as our time is limited, may I ask you once again: Did you report him to Mr. Meakic, and was he punished by his removal, as you stated in this statement, or what you said today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I said today; that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, madam. I have no further questions. I would like you to forget this as soon as possible and that we can all go back to normal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Simic. I think you took a little more than 20 minutes. Have you -- does that mean that you have cross-examined for Mr. Fila as well? No. I see that Mr. Fila is coming, so Mr. Simic hasn't taken his time. Mr. Fila, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Fila. Microphone is not switched on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You've had enough trouble. I don't want to trouble you too much. You mentioned that you knew Mr. Radic. During your stay in Omarska, did he bring you some food, pies and things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he treat you humanely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there a hot plate in the office where he was working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was something for cooking coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you have coffee with him when he was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whenever I made coffee, I would get a cupful as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there a toilet or a bathroom upstairs, or at least a toilet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you use it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could that window be moved, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was opened like this, towards you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What could you see through that window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could see the area in front of the garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where the buses halted, came to a stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That area could be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you use the toilet in the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know somebody called Bozidar Markovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was there somebody you called your guardian angel over there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who stood in front of the area where the women were detained, by somebody's orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a position where there was a guard watching over the women when we went to sleep. There was a position there.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you know that person as Bozidar Markovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The composition of the shifts -- you said there were three of them -- was it always the same? Did they switch from one shift to another? That is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you talking about the guards?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, the guards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know who decided who would work in which shift within the shift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you think Radic could have determined that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If those people were in Radic's shift, such as they were, did he select them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I give an explanation in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I am not in a hurry, but we all are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that Mladjo Radic was a policeman before the war as well, and I think that all those boys saw Radic as a more important person than Milojica and Momir Gruban.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That was not my question. Who designated those boys to work with Mladjo? Did Mladjo do that? Radic, could he say, "I want so-and-so to work in my shift"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But you were talking about the authority of a former policeman, of a regular policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When this incident occurred with the beating and bread falling out, (redacted), where were you when you complained to Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the kitchen. In the kitchen. It wasn't just that incident. It wasn't just that. But we spoke in the kitchen. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have any negative consequences as a result of your complaint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: From him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. But what was happening to those people. It was so painful.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, no. My question is: The fact that you complained to him, did you personally have any negative consequences as a result of complaining to Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why didn't you complain to him about this Soskan then? If his name was Soskan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I wanted to forget about it as soon as possible. I didn't want to think about it. He was a young man. I could have almost been his mother. So I wanted to reject the whole incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But the reason wasn't that you feared Mladjo Radic and the consequences upon you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Where were you when you saw that event on St. Peter's Day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the restaurant. I'd like to show it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was it in the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan promised to bring a pointer and he hasn't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That night when it happened, I left my room.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you say "room," tell us where that is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the upper floor where we slept. I passed by the room where the other women slept. I entered the office where the guard post was for the guard watching the women and there was no one there, and I entered -- I'd love to show it to you. Then I entered this first room for interrogation. I looked through the window, because this had already been shown to me. I went through the window to where the machine-gun was next to the wall, and that is how I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought I turned it on. I think Exhibit 3/28, which is a photograph of the buildings from the outside, might assist Mr. Fila, and she can use that on the ELMO to point where she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I just didn't wish to waist time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila has already gone over that. But thank you very much, Mr. Keegan, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as there was no identification of the accused, may I ask the witness whether she recognises Mladjo Radic in this courtroom and who he is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have seen the witness recognise him very well, but go ahead, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: If you have recognised him, there's no need.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all. Thank you, Your Honour. I've finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. Objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, towards the end of Mr. Fila's cross, you said that the witness had recognised the accused well. However, we expect the Prosecution to show the photo board on which the witness did not positively identify Mr. Kvocka. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, I apologise. Please come back and carry out the formal recognition by Witness B of Mr. Radic. That is clear. I think there is something non-verbal that is an English body language which is very clear, but please go ahead, Mr. Fila, from the formal standpoint, but we Judges are watching with attention. At least I speak on my own behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Madam, will you please tell us, from the door, not counting the gentlemen in uniform, who is Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first man next to the man in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just one more question. Did you see or hear him after you left Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I called him once. I just asked them how they were. It was just a formality. And I saw him after his arrest, on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Mr. Jovan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: We have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your colleagues have done the work for you. So that's good. Mr. Keegan, do you have any re-examination, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes. Just briefly please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, you were asked questions by Mr. Simic regarding Mr. Zoran Delic and whether he was only present in the camp when food was served. Now, were you ever interrogated in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was the last to be interrogated in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your objection, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My objection, Mr. President, is that in the course of the cross-examination, neither Mr. Fila nor I mentioned the witness' interrogation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I agree. However, if my colleague will allow me, I was laying a foundation to see who was present at the interrogation, and that was the only question I was going to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but Mr. Keegan -- no. Go on to another question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I'll make it more clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you see Zoran Delic at anyplace in the camp other than the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was there when I was being interrogated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There you are, Mr. Simic. You can learn a little. There's always a way of getting round things. So formalities are always a little complicated. This is a good example. Thank you, Mr. Keegan. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You were asked questions by Mr. Simic about Zeljko Meakic's reaction when you reported to him that the prisoners had been beaten on that day that you described here in the courtroom, not that they were on strike, and you were asked, "Did he say anything?" or that he undertook any action. Did the beatings at lunch, at the meal time, continue after your conversations with Mr. Meakic, that is, for the remaining time in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After this conversation with Mr. Meakic, it was a little, a little better. There were less beatings, less mistreatment, and even they gave them a little more time to enter, eat, and get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, Witness B, how long were you in the camp? Until what date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the 23rd of August, 1991 -- 1992. I'm sorry, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you recall -- in your testimony earlier, you referred to the visit of the journalists and that the women were not allowed to be present.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you recall the date of that visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You referred to a conversation with Zeljko Meakic when he asked you and Velida Mahmuljin if you'd had any problems in the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You indicated that was at the end of your stay in the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He called the two of us, as I said. They asked us whether we had any problems, because we had spent the longest period of time there, whether we had problems, mistreatment. I said no. However, Velida told him about the incident when she was taken out and everything that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, this conversation, was this just prior to you leaving the camp on 23 August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was just before the camp was disbanded or, rather, when people were divided up into groups, first, second, and third category of detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Earlier you talked about there was a change in conditions near the end of the time in the camp. Are you able to say with certainty whether those changes occurred at any time before the journalists visited or after? Can you say with certainty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say with certainty after the visit of journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Fila asked you some questions about Mladjo Radic's shift, and you indicated that the boys, as you called them, saw Radic as a more important person because he'd been a regular policeman before the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If one of those guards was abusing a detainee and Mladjo Radic ordered him to stop, in your opinion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Mr. Fila, what is your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is being repeated. It has been asked; if Mladjo Radic ordered, what would have happen, and you have that in the transcript, asked and answered. The question is being repeated in order to obtain a different answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and the answer was that they would obey. So I remember that. You have the answer, Mr. Keegan.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not all. Not all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Keegan, go on, please. Don't repeat the question. Go on to another question. You know how to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I wasn't going to ask the same question. I was asking a very specific, following up on the information which the witness now elicited on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If Mladjo Radic was present when a guard was abusing a detainee and Mladjo Radic ordered him to stop, in your opinion, would that guard stop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he would, because after all, Mladjo Radic was responsible, and I think he had some kind of way of influencing the members of his shift.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, I saw you on your feet. What is the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are all assumptions. If he had been present, if he had seen, if there had been a beating, if he had ordered what would have happened. This is in meteorology, in the weather forecast and not in practice, legal practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a sense you are right, if it is a hypothesis -- it is a hypothesis, but you know well that the Judges may know how to make a distinction between when something was done and when something is a hypothesis and when the witness gives only opinion. So the Judges know how to make a distinction. He was trying to find out who would obey and who would not obey, but it is a hypothesis. Mr. Keegan, so go on to the matter directly with clear and concise questions. That is what I keep repeating. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, you were also asked some questions about whether there was any medical personnel who visited the camp. You referred to Dr. Ivic and a medical technician Mico, who had one arm. When you saw them in the camp, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would come there. They would go to the police room. I didn't see them treating anyone. I didn't see them giving them any kind of medical aid that they might need. I didn't see them check up on the health of the prisoners. I didn't see any of those things done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we now have shown to the witness what we have marked as Exhibit 3/89A and B, which is the Witness' 1994 statement that's been referred to in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Witness B, you have there a statement in both the English and Bosnian languages. If you can look on the English-language version one. Does your statement appear on the first page of that document? I'm sorry, does your signature appear? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, quite obvious it is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And do you recall giving this statement to members of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And I believe it was already elicited on cross-examination that you gave that statement freely and voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: This statement in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Yes. Yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And can you look at the last page of the English version, please, and indicate if your signature also appears there on the acknowledgement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would offer Exhibit 39 -- oh, not yet. Sorry, Your Honour. We should conclude your questions, first. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan, perhaps I should have taken this into consideration earlier on, but you sent us Exhibit 3/88A, B, and C, but I don't think you used Exhibit C.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness described that the pictures were of the house; and specifically, one was of the street, one was of the house before the war, and one was after, when it was destroyed. I believe that's in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Keegan. You just asked to have admitted the witness's whole statement, which is a long statement with a lot of material in it. I don't even what know -- we don't have any underlined portions or any indicated portions. I don't know what part of it you're suggesting and for what reason you think it should be admitted. You certainly are familiar with the debate, which we'll consider at greater length at the Status Conference, as to whether or not, when you have one contradiction, you can get an entire witness's statement in, or whether it's only allowed in for the purpose of illustrating the contradiction. So maybe, at least for me, you can elucidate on what basis you're admitting that long statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I pulled back from that because I recall that we were supposed to wait until, indeed, after your questions to actually offer the admissions, and I would have carried out the full discussion then. I'm happy to do it now if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, it's just a brief, because, I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point there is no decision on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Under our rules, of course here at the Tribunal, the Judges are free to consider all relevant evidence. It's up to you to decide what part of that statement you would find relevant once you make your decision. It's our position if they challenge a witness on a statement, they can't escape the inevitable by failing to show that witness the statement and ask them if they agree if that's what it says -- indeed, they don't even do -- to then try and use that as an excuse to keep the whole statement out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No, I understand the whole statement, but obviously you're also familiar with the practice in many jurisdictions with which we're both familiar, that you identify the portion that you want to put in to show what's relevant or why their particular portion was not the only one that was relevant. But you don't get to put in a book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That is true, Your Honour, but I'm also aware in those same jurisdictions there's a rule of completeness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And the Court can then decide what parts it may or may not accept. And I'm also aware that in other jurisdictions in the world, in fact the whole statement would be considered, because it's all part of the witness's evidence. And so I think that obviously is a decision that will have to be made by this Chamber at a later date, when we have the full discussion, and of course at that point the Chamber can then decide what, if any, portions it's going to give weight to or accept as full evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, it certainly would have been helpful if you would have indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I was going to, but at the end, Your Honour. I pulled it back because I realised I was out of sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now we move to the Judges' questions. Mr. Simic, we are passing on to the Judges' questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The accused cannot speak here. They will be given an opportunity to speak. But I have noted on several occasions there has been communication between the accused and the counsel. The counsel know very well, full well, what their duty is. Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence at this point wishes to tender documents which it has received from the Prosecution. They are incomplete, however. One document shows that the lady, B, Witness B, did not make a positive identification of Mr. Kvocka, regardless of the meetings and the events she has recounted. But we only have the photos of other -- boards of other individuals, and that is why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, I apologise for interrupting. I do apologise. Perhaps I'll be a little harsh on you, but do you know what it means, work organisation, and how to organise work? We have just said that we're going to treat the tendering of documents in the file at the end of Judges' questions. Have you understood that?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please do respect our moment, the Judges' question time, and I give the floor to Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Witness B, good afternoon. I would like to get some more clarifications from you, if you can. After listening carefully to your very clear testimony, I wanted to -- I gathered from your testimony that several people were really in command of the camp. First, you said that Kvocka was treated as -- I'll try to find your words, but it doesn't matter -- as responsible of the commandment and had important functions in the camp, and that the guards called him "chief." Then, when you spoke about Prcac, you said that he had the same functions as Kvocka, and also you said that Meakic affirmed, I think, when you asked him, affirmed that Prcac was the commander of the camp and that he was the head of the security. So could you -- then can I -- can we understand from that there are three commanders equal, which are Kvocka, and which are Prcac, and which are Meakic? Is that what you said or what I understood? On equal footing?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But Radic was not among them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I said that during my time there -- could you repeat the first name you mentioned? Zeljko Meakic -- Miroslav Kvocka, yes. Miroslav Kvocka. During the Kvocka Miroslav time, I said that he said the function for which Zeljko Meakic told me after, for Drago Prcac, who had come to replace Miroslav Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So he replaced Kvocka, and Radic was less than them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But Radic was the head of a team, head of a shift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And he was obeyed by this shift? That's a question. Was he obeyed by the shift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, this shift, there was this Predojevic who apparently was violent, more violent than the others, was this man some kind of above the law, or was he acting in line with all this -- with the policy of the whole team?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what policy this refers to, but all I know is that that young man was a raging animal in the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, this leads me to the second question. Do you think any of these people, whether the commanders, Kvocka, Prcac, or Radic, if they said no, if they asked for someone to stop, would they be obeyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they would, but that is just my assumption, that they would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Were there incidents where they asked somebody to stop, or somebody to do something, or incidents where they were not obeyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't notice that at all, had they said "No" or "Don't do that." I didn't see that ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So in other words, none of the people in control interfered to stop any beating or torture, or whatever happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, my other question is concerned -- I'm sorry to ask you -- this abuse you mentioned. Were there other ladies abused, apart from the experience which happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's difficult to say for another woman, another person, woman. And it is not up to me. I cannot speak for other women. Can I say something now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were those who were abused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because you mentioned the example of Velida, but you didn't go ahead -- you said that you concluded from her silence and her pain that she was abused.
