utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Then you mentioned also that when you went by mistake -- I think it was by mistake -- to Radic's room, he told you he was waiting for Jadranka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Jadranka, and what did you gather from that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that Jadranka was in the same situation as I was. She was a prisoner. Whether she came there or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you said he told you something about her.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want me to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, please, if it gives any clarity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he said something along these lines: that he was waiting for Jadranka to get his own back on her. Now, what kind of retribution, I don't know. It's difficult for me to say. And I'm a woman. It's not simple for me to talk about things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was she a prisoner, Jadranka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That's all. Now, there is finally just a question. One of the pictures, 3/70D, with an old man walking, going into the restaurant, a man who could be in a very advanced age. Did they have old people in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, judging by their appearance, they were about between 65 and 70 years old. And this is obvious from the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It's obvious that the man is much older than that. So they might get older in the camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions of the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Were there children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were minors as well. Yes, under age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Under age. What do you call "under age"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under the age of 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Under the age of 18. Thank you very much, Witness B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I have only one question. In the beginning of your testimony, when you said that your neighbours, who had been listening to the radio, said that instructions had come to go on, to abandon their homes and move on to the centre of the village, did your neighbours tell you that those instructions on the radio came from any particular source? Was it military, was it civilian? Was it the Serbs who were taken over? Was it the old TO? How did the source identify itself, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That information came via Radio Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But it didn't say -- did you know at that time, or did they know, who controlled Radio Prijedor at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness B, I have just one question to ask you. The Prosecutor asked you their questions, the Defence asked you questions. Is there anything that you should like to say which hasn't been raised yet, which nobody has asked you yet, and you'd like to talk about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are a lot of things that I'd like to say in conclusion, but I find it very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Take your time, Witness. We have great respect for the suffering you have had, all of us here. So please do take your time and feel at ease.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I shall try, nonetheless, to say something. After all the tragedies that happened over there, it is very difficult for me to say, and I can never say that I'm happy or will be happy. I lost my father, I lost my sister. My daughter has great difficulties after everything, and so do I myself. I have a lot of problems. I'm just asking myself who had the right to take me from my home, from my country too, so that I am a refugee, a displaced person in the world? Who had the right to do all this? And I hope that nonetheless the person who did that will be punished, both by God and by you, and that you will give them just sentence for what they did. So much for me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness B. We are here to try and do that, and independently of the responsible people, all the things that happened to you and to the other people, we do not differentiate between ethnicity and nationality. We know that everybody suffered in one way or another. But we shall do our utmost to do something. And you yourself have given your own contribution, and let me say, you did it courageously, and we should like to express our deep gratitude to you for your coming here. You can stay there, before you leave, to put the protective measures in place. And in the meantime, we shall be tendering documents and exhibits. Mr. Usher, the witness remains where she is. I think that if we draw the blinds, that the witness could leave the courtroom. Because, madam, I think you should have a good rest now. Thank you once again for coming, Witness B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Admission into evidence. First of all, I should like to say that I have noticed that one of the accused communicated aloud with the counsel, and I have said that he has no right to do that. You understood the context. Of course, the accused can communicate with the Defence, but the Chamber can prevent it from being done in that manner. And I think that the accused understand what I meant. So I have nothing further to say. As for admission into evidence, Mr. Keegan, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution would offer into evidence Exhibits 3/27 and 3/24 [sic], which were the photos of Keraterm Camp; Exhibit 3/31, which was the photograph of the man with the bruises; Exhibit 3/70A through D, which was the four photographs of the prisoners going in to get the meal and leaving the canteen; Exhibit 3/69A and B, which were the photographs of Mladjo Radic and Drazenko Predojevic, and the uniforms; exhibit 3/88A, B, and C, which were the photographs of the witness' house; and Exhibit 3/89A and B, the witness' statement. I'm advised, Your Honour, that the transcript said "3/24" for one of the photographs for Keraterm. It should be 3/34. So 27 and 34. Unless I'm corrected by my colleagues, Your Honour, I think that's all of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan, just to speed things up, you understood well, I think, what Mr. Simic is going to ask, the document you are familiar with. To speed things up, can you tell us something straight away? Can you respond before Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We provided the Defence all relevant photo boards which any of the witnesses have viewed, and we have no objection if the Defence wants to offer the photo boards and the documents which indicate the results of those photo boards. So we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Simic, for going ahead a little, but I think we understood what your motion was. So do you have any objection to the admission of the exhibits tendered by the Prosecution and your own suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I speak only in my own name. Regarding all the exhibits, that is, photographs, we have no objections. However, as regards the admission of the statements of Witness B, we do have an objection, because in the materials, we received another statement in B/C/S. There is no date or anything else. This is a statement that differs considerably, and it was not tendered by the Prosecution today. It has a number on it but not a proper exhibit number. As for our suggestion to tender documents, it is true that the Prosecution has been providing us photo boards for identification. Unfortunately, as far as Witness B is concerned, we were given a list of all persons who did carry out identification, and on this list it is clearly evident that Witness B did not recognise Mr. Kvocka on the photograph offered to her. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, are you asking for this document to be admitted? Don't make any allegations about the document; just ask for its admission. Do you understand the distinction?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honour. But I want to tell you, Your Honour, that the Prosecution did not give us the photo board linked to this case, this identification, so we can only tender as evidence a list confirming -- or a document confirming that Witness B did not identify Mr. Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan, any objection to the admission of 3/99A and B, statement of the witness? And why did the Defence not receive this document, as Mr. Simic has just told us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I cannot confirm that the Defence did not receive it. This has been an ongoing problem, Your Honour. We have recently sent letters to the Defence reminding them we have the obligation to disclose. When we do disclose, we provide receipts which we request the Defence to sign and return, and if they are not provided with something on the list, to note that on the receipt. Unfortunately, the Defence counsel, in large -- well, in almost all circumstances, have failed to return these receipts. So until they do so, we can't confirm whether they received something or not. We will certainly provide another copy to the Court and allow for its admission into evidence at the next hearing if Mr. Simic, in fact, can confirm he did not receive it. We would be happy to do that. But although, of course, we have the obligation to disclose, we believe they have the obligation to account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Mr. Simic was speaking in his own name. I still haven't heard the reaction of the other Defence counsel regarding the admission of these exhibits. Mr. Nikolic's team. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might, just before Mr. O'Sullivan speaks. With respect to the issue raised by Mr. Simic about another statement, he was at liberty to offer it and we certainly have no objection to its admission, the second statement that he's referred to. Once we can see the document and, in fact, see that it is the statement of Witness B, we would have no objection to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Sullivan. Just a moment, please, Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regards to all the exhibits, with the exception of Witness B's statement, we have no objections. We do object to a procedure by which previous out-of-court statements are admitted in their entirety. Your Honours, I submit that previous statements used during cross-examination and put to a witness for confrontation are used for impeachment purposes only, and in my submission, they're admissible -- their admissibility is limited to the impeachment, and the statement in it's entirety is not admissible. The procedure I've just described was used in the Celebici trial. I submit it should be adopted and followed in these proceedings. It's good law in this Tribunal, it's sound law, and it ensures that Your Honours can make a fair determination of the issues. The Trial Chamber hears a witness viva voce, and if that witness is confronted with a previous out-of-court statement, that can allow Your Honours to judge issues such as credibility of that witness and weight you accord to his or her testimony. So our submission is that witness statements used during cross-examination are admissible for the limited purposes of impeachment and for no other reason. Those are my submissions on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, without repeating what has just been said, I support what Mr. O'Sullivan has said, as well as the position I presented yesterday, that if a statement is admitted, then it applies only to the person who cross-examined and not to the other Defence counsel. I also object to the admission of Exhibit 3/31. It is a photograph of a man with something red all over his body. I never saw such a red-coloured body, and I don't know whether this is red paint or whether these are really bruises. And where would it end if we were all to bring photographs of this kind to the courtroom. On several occasions, this Trial Chamber has referred to its intelligence and the intelligence of all of us, and I'm sure all of us know what bruises look like, and they don't look like this. Not as red as this, anyway. Therefore, I object in principle. I have admitted that there were beatings in the Omarska camp. So let me make it clear: There were bruises, but tendering this type of evidence will not lead us anywhere. I am not denying that you are right, that there were beatings, but I do object to this photograph. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But excuse me, Mr. Fila. You accept the admission of this document, coupled with your reservations?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I am told where this photograph was taken, who is on the photograph. Did he belonged to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tosic. Please don't repeat what others have said, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. I'll do my best. We have no objection to the admission of the documents tendered by the Prosecution, except we support colleague O'Sullivan and my learned friend Mr. Fila, without repeating what they have said. And secondly, also regarding Mr. Simic's tendering of documents, because from the exhibit, it is clear that Witness B did not recognise our client, and as this is the same document where our client is mentioned, we too would like to support Mr. Simic's suggestion that that list of identification be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tosic. Mr. Jovan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're opposed to the admission of the statement, and we support the objections of our colleague O'Sullivan and Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Jovan Simic. I think Mr. Krstan Simic had something to add, but before I give the floor to Mr. Keegan, I had a feeling you had something to add, Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one sentence. I would ask that a photo board for Mr. Kvocka be attached to this. Mr. Zigic is there too. We have the photo boards, but we do not have the photo board for Mr. Kvocka, so could it be attached? Your Honour, I have a feeling that there's some confusion here. It is not disputed that the Prosecution has disclosed to us a report and three photo boards linked to the identification of certain persons. Also, the Prosecution has disclosed to us another document with a list of all the persons who were identified, and under number 21, Witness B confirmed that she did not recognise Mr. Kvocka. However, the technical problem is that the only document lacking is the photo board, and we appeal to the Prosecution to attach that photo board and then there will be no confusion and no problems. The problem will be solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Keegan, I was thinking that since we're already late, perhaps we can admit all the uncontested documents and then we can take up the matter when we resume the hearings during the discussion. Perhaps that would be better. So if you can give us an idea of your response, because there was some concrete matters requested by Mr. Simic, otherwise, we will not go on with this debate. Do you agree with this plan at first glance, with this suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, that Ms. Hollis would like to answer this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we agree with your suggestion. The concrete plan regarding the specific exhibits that Mr. Simic is requesting, the Defence were given a variety of affidavits from the chief investigator of Team 1, indicating that in certain circumstances, photo boards were not kept when a witness failed to identify someone. The affidavits also indicated that there was a failure to identify. Now, again because we don't know, based on Mr. Simic's assertions alone, whether he received that document or not, and I haven't had sufficient time to go through our receipts to see if he did receive it, I can't at this moment say whether he was given that affidavit. It is my understanding that those affidavits were severed on Defence counsel, and certainly reports were served on them to show that there were failures to identify these individuals. So I will verify that those were served. To the extent that they were not, I will certainly make them available, but it's my understanding that they were served. And we agree that the issue of these statements is an issue that should be taken up at a later time, because we believe that it is a significant issue and would warrant some discussion. So we do agree that things that are not contested would be admitted at this time, and we would deal with contested matters at the next hearing. We would, perhaps, take this opportunity to ask the Court to perhaps make their position known about whether they would ask the Defence to please make an effort to check the material we give them, sign the receipts in a timely fashion, return them to us, and tell us what's missing. We don't think that's unfair. We do believe, in fact, that's an obligation. We go to great trouble to give them very itemised receipts and they very seldom return them. Some return them much more frequently than others and we appreciate that, but for the most part, we haven't gotten them back, and that makes it easier for them to stand up and say, "We were never given it." So we would ask for some assistance with that perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're admitting into evidence the exhibits that were not contested, and the others, we will resume the discussion on them at a later stage. I'm saying this because we don't have time to continue this discussion. I hope you understand. Before adjourning, I should like to follow on what Ms. Hollis has just said, to see whether you have indeed received or not something. Maybe this is something we should discuss at a Status Conference, that is, the organisation of work by the Defence, because in my opinion, allow me to speak very frankly, there is a lot to be done outside the courtroom, and I fear that the Defence will one day come and say, "We need time to do such-and-such a thing." As far as the Prosecution is concerned, I wish to tell you that we really have to think over all the initial ideas about summaries, seven days' advanced notice, et cetera, et cetera. We really must make sure that the Defence has received, seven days in advance, lists of witnesses and these things, and this is a reciprocal issue. It applies to both sides. As we're going to have a recess in this case, I should like to think that this stage was truly exceptional. I would like us to resume the case with a completely different dynamics, when things will flow easily, when everyone will accomplish its duties of a disclosure. You know that we have come to the conclusion that we must make a distinction between the time for the hearings, precisely to respect witnesses coming here. When I talk about witnesses, I always say that the Defence or the Prosecution, be they Serb, Croats, or others, they are persons who come here, and I wish to tell you that the Chamber will be extremely vigilant regarding the respect we owe the witnesses and which we must guarantee to them. And in order to respect those witnesses, we must really make the best of the time for the hearings and separate the time for our own discussions. I do not wish to interrupt you, but we must organise the way we speak. Otherwise, you yourself will understand that we will not achieve our goals. The first day of the next hearings, I'm telling you that we will be having a Status Conference a day or two later, which is necessary to regulate the conduct of the proceedings. I just now wish to wish you all the best in your work -- we are all going to work and not rest -- and have a good weekend, all of you. I must now thank the interpreters and the technical booth for agreeing, though involuntarily, to work overtime. But in any event, I thank you all for making your services available for us to finish our work today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: at 3.38 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 5th day of June, 2000 at 9.30 a.m.
